summary:
Caldas stands under the national framework of Colombia, where legal gender recognition rests on self-recognition. Since a rule change approved in June 2015, trans Colombians change the sex marker on government-issued identification by signing a document before a notary, replacing the earlier route in which judges ordered bodily inspections or psychiatric assessments. Constitutional Court jurisprudence dating from 1993 recognises legal gender recognition without a surgical requirement, and national identification documents have carried "trans" and "non-binary" markers since November 2025.

The violence picture this department is assessed against is national. El País English edition reported on 14 April 2025 that Sara Millerey, a 32-year-old trans woman, was beaten in broad daylight in Bello, Antioquia, filmed by onlookers and thrown into a creek; she died of a second cardiac arrest the following afternoon and no one had been arrested. The same report states that hate crimes killed 13 trans people in Colombia in the first quarter of 2025, and that her death provoked national outrage and mobilisations against transphobia.

Some of the targeting is organised and state recording of it is contested. The Guardian reported on 30 July 2024 that armed groups in Caquetá gave trans woman Tatiana Cespedes one week to leave town or be killed and circulated "social cleansing" flyers against trans women; an activist quoted in the investigation said the prosecutor's office does not recognise transfemicide, recording the killings as ordinary cases. The investigation counts 41 trans women killed in Colombia in 2023 and eight between February and April 2024.

No finding specific to Caldas on law, enforcement practice or incidents affecting trans people appears in the sources available for this record. The reporting carried here is national in scope or concerns other departments, and nothing in it marks Caldas as materially safer or more dangerous than the country as a whole. A visitor to Caldas should therefore expect the national framework on paper and the national pattern of violence in practice, with no local evidence either way.
tangentialFactors:
The gap between formal protection and recorded outcomes is a documented feature of the national picture rather than a local one: Colombia's identification rules, Constitutional Court jurisprudence and administrative decrees sit alongside a count of 41 trans women killed in 2023 and 13 in the first quarter of 2025.

Armed-group activity and "social cleansing" campaigns are recorded in departments other than Caldas, notably Caquetá, where displacement of trans women away from home towns is a reported outcome rather than an incidental one. Whether comparable armed-group presence in Caldas produces comparable risk is not addressed by these sources.
localsOnly:
Trans Colombians change the sex marker on government-issued identification by signing a document before a notary, and national identification documents have carried "trans" and "non-binary" markers since November 2025. Constitutional Court jurisprudence from 1993 recognises recognition on the basis of self-recognition without a surgical requirement.

An activist quoted in July 2024 reporting states that the prosecutor's office does not recognise transfemicide as such, recording killings of trans women as ordinary cases, which affects how residents' deaths are classified and pursued.
outOfScopeNotes:
No Caldas-specific source on enforcement practice, police conduct, facilities access, healthcare access or documented incidents affecting trans people was available for this record; the department's position on those questions is unresolved rather than negative.

Whether the prosecutor's-office recording practice described in national reporting is applied in Caldas in the same way is not sourced here.

The outcome of the Millerey case beyond the arrest status reported on 14 April 2025, and any later national homicide counts for 2025, are not carried in the available inventory.
